The Russet sparrow Passer cinnamomeus is a medium-sized passerine that exhibits a set of well-defined life-history traits typical of temperate-zone members of the family Passeridae. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days], an incubation period that aligns closely with values reported for the closely related Eurasian tree sparrow Passer montanus, on which this estimate is partially based. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge with a wet body mass averaging just 1.79 grams [Wwb = 1.79 grams], reflecting the considerable yolk reserves that are rapidly metabolized during the first days of brooding. This neonatal mass stands in stark contrast to the initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, which has been recorded at 2.05 grams [Ww0 = 2.05 grams], indicating that the embryo consumes a substantial fraction of the albumen and yolk during its 13-day developmental period. The energetic demands placed on the incubating female are therefore considerable, as she must maintain the clutch at the precise thermal optimum required for normal embryogenesis.

As the chicks progress through the nestling phase, their growth trajectory is rapid, fueled by intensive biparental provisioning of insect prey. Under thermoneutral conditions approximating the active metabolic state of adults, which correspond to a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young achieve the capacity for sustained flight at a remarkably early age. Specifically, fledging, defined as the point at which the nestling attains sufficient wing and flight muscle development to leave the nest and perform its first sustained flight, occurs at 16 days after hatching [tx = 16 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of many small-bodied passerines that face high predation risk in the nest. Following nest departure, the fledglings remain dependent on parental feeds for several additional days while their flight feathers complete maturation and their foraging skills improve. The rapid mass gain during the nestling phase is essential for building the energy reserves needed to survive the vulnerable post-fledging period of independence.

Sexual maturation in the Russet sparrow proceeds along a predictable timeline when birds are maintained under standard captive conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal steroidogenesis and the first observable development of secondary sexual characteristics, is attained at 48 days after hatching [tp = 48 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively early maturation reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid attainment of reproductive potential, a common pattern among small, short-lived passerines that experience high annual adult mortality. Following the onset of puberty, young birds undergo a period of behavioral and physiological refinement before they are ready to initiate their first breeding attempt. The time elapsed from birth to the production of the first brood is considerably longer than the age at sexual maturity itself, owing to the need to secure a territory, form a pair bond, and complete the necessary pre-breeding molt. Field studies have demonstrated that under optimal thermal conditions, this milestone is typically reached at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals do not breed successfully until their second calendar year at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, a feature that is consistent across many members of the genus Passer. Females, which are the larger sex, reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 19.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 19.6 grams], whereas adult males attain a slightly lower asymptotic mass averaging 16.6 grams [Wwi = 16.6 grams]. This dimorphism is thought to be driven by the energetic demands of egg production and incubation in females, which favor a larger body frame capable of storing greater reserves. In contrast, the smaller male body mass may confer advantages in aerial agility during territorial defense and courtship displays. These mass values represent the maximum recorded wet weights for healthy, free-living adults measured during the non-breeding season, when body condition is not influenced by the reproductive effort. Foraging studies indicate that the birds are able to maintain these weights on a diet composed primarily of small seeds and invertebrates, with seasonal shifts in prey availability driving modest fluctuations in body condition.

The maximum reproductive rate of the Russet sparrow has been estimated from long-term nest monitoring programs and captive colony data collected at a stable ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Females typically produce between 2 and 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 6 eggs per clutch], with a mean clutch size that varies latitudinally, and they are capable of raising up to two broods annually [F_R_i = up to two broods annually] under favorable conditions. This combination of moderate clutch size and multiple brooding results in a substantial annual fecundity that offsets the relatively short lifespan of the species. The maximum recorded longevity for the Russet sparrow, again based on data extrapolated from the closely related Passer montanus monitored under controlled thermal regimes, reaches approximately 13.1 years [am = approximately 13.1 years] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. While few individuals in wild populations attain this age due to predation, disease, and environmental stochasticity, the physiological potential for such extended survival underscores the species' capacity for reproductive output over a prolonged adult lifetime, a lifespan that places it among the longer-lived members of the genus Passer.
